Specifically, this line is Ken Carson talking about his own evolution:

“Teen X” → his earlier era/persona (he literally had a project called Teen X and was known as “Teen X” early on)

“X-Man” → his newer, upgraded identity — more mature, confident, and established

So he’s saying:

“I used to be the young version of myself, but now I’ve grown into a stronger, next-level version.”

It’s self-referencing + rebranding, not about another person.
Artists do this a lot to mark growth and power shifts in their career.

he also talks a same idea that  shows up in his song “Evolution,” but in a broader, more conceptual way.

He’s still talking about personal growth and leveling up, just not with the exact “Teen X → X-Man” name flip.

In “Evolution”, the focus is on:

Changing as a person and artist

Rising status and success

Outgrowing his old situation, mindset, and limits

Becoming a more powerful, established version of himself

So its like this:

“Teen X → X-Man” = a specific bar showing growth through wordplay

“Evolution” = the overall theme of transformation, progression, and upgrade

They’re connected ideas:

I used to be one thing, now I’m something bigger.

He’s reinforcing his brand narrative: constant evolution, never staying the same.

Threat imagery, not literal plans

Very common in hype rap

Don’t disrespect me — I’m not weak.

Not: here’s what I actually do.

His style, confidence, and image influence others.

They was like believing in what I was doing[…]

meaning:
Ken’s presenting an extreme persona — dangerous, grown, rich, and still connected to the streets — to show he’s fully left his “kid” phase behind.

Line by line:

“In New York, I ride with the machete”
This is intimidation imagery. He’s saying he moves like someone you shouldn’t mess with. It’s about projecting toughness, not literal day-to-day behavior.

“It’s X-Man, fuck all that teen shit”
He’s rejecting his younger ‘Teen X’ identity and emphasizing that he’s now fully grown, hardened, and more powerful.

“But I still pour codeine in my beverage”
This keeps the rockstar / reckless image. It’s about excess and rebellion — part of the persona — not a how-to.

“I got rich, but I’m still servin’ fiends”
This is contradiction on purpose: even with money, he claims he hasn’t fully left his past behind. It reinforces the idea of being both successful and street-connected.

“If you out of town, you know I’ma mail it”
This exaggerates reach and influence — saying his operation goes beyond one place. Again, this is bragging, not logistics.

“Ain’t no coppin’ no less than a P”
“P” is slang for a large amount. He’s saying he deals only in big quantities, which signals higher status.

“I’m servin’ these pounds, I ain’t gotta scale it”
This means he’s so experienced and big-time that he doesn’t need to measure — another confidence flex.

What it REALLY means overall:

I’m no longer a kid, I’m powerful, feared, rich, and still connected to the gritty world I came from.

This kind of verse is about image and dominance, not realism. Rappers often compress years of experiences into one exaggerated character to make the song hit harder.

line: I’m havin’ Franklins, not Kirk
vault_lines: I'm havin' Franklins, not Kirk
meaning:
Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States, appears on the $100 bill. Ken is saying that he has hundreds on hundreds of dollars.

On the other hand, Kirk Franklin is a gospel artist. You might’ve seen him before.

This line is NOT a double entendre. Around two months before the release of this song, popular right-wing political activist and media personality Charlie Kirk was assassinated. As a result, the US Congress introduced the Charlie Kirk Commemorative Coin Act, which planned to mint and circulate 400,000 one-dollar coins (made of silver) with a portrait of Kirk on it.

Contrary to what some people think, it is highly unlikely that Ken is referencing this, because:
1) Using our context clues, this song seems to be recorded in or around 2023-2024, or early 2025 at the latest, way before Kirk’s assassination.
2) As of this song’s release, Charlie Kirk’s coin isn’t anywhere close to being minted, or even passed in Congress.
3) Benjamin Franklin and Kirk Franklin share the same last name, and Ken has to specify which one he’s talking about. Which is why he said “not Kirk,” instead of “not Kirks,” which would’ve suggested that he was talking about the coins.

Media Literacy is important, folks. Just because something or someone is vaguely related by name does not mean it’s a double entendre.

line: Upside-down cross on my neck, they think it’s blasphemy
vault_lines: Upside-down cross on my neck, they think it's blasphemy
meaning:
The label that Ken is under, Opium, has long been associated with “Satanic” imagery, and most notably, all of the members under the label have a chain with an upside-down cross to signify that they are part of Opium.

Additionally, on Ken’s 2023 song Rockstar Lifestyle, he says:

Upside down cross what’s on my neck, but I ain’t never sell my soul

The wider audience has been split about whether or not the cross necklace was “Satanic” or just St. Peter’s cross. In a interview with Pitchfork in 2024, Ken explained that the upside down cross was a reference to the biblical figure “Saint Peter,” stating,

“Saint Peter felt less worthy than Jesus and I feel the same way. I’m no God why would I come to you as if I am.”

However, many listeners interpret the symbol differently, believing that Opium or at least Playboi Carti intended the cross to align with the labels broader “Satanic” imagery. As a result, the “Opium” aesthetic is often seen as being shaped by Carti’s recurring use of Satanic inspired symbolism rather than by traditional religious meaning.

Here, Carti lays on a pentagram. This was taken around the Whole Lotta Red era.

Carti’s tattoo reads “Satan”, taken in 2022.

Additionally, Ken has shown himself with a (fake?)  tattoo of a pentagram, in late 2024.


Regardless, all of this is just artistic expression for a dated aesthetic. It does not mean they actually believe any of it.

“AP” refers to Audemars Piguet, the Swiss luxury watchmaker, while Rick refers to fashion designer Rick Owens.

Audemars Piguet itself uses “AP” throughout its branding—including its AP Houses—and Rick Owens is particularly associated with luxury footwear and clothing.

Ken is describing mixing luxury labels in one outfit: an Audemars Piguet watch paired with Rick Owens clothing, which fits the song’s central theme of shopping and assembling expensive designer looks.

Rather than simply saying somebody was an old friend, he gives a very specific childhood test: if they weren’t close enough to sit together at lunch, he doesn’t consider them someone who really came up with him.

This line uses “spiked” as a double meaning.

To spike a drink means to add another substance to it. In football, a quarterback (QB) can also spike the ball, intentionally throwing it directly into the ground, most commonly to stop a running game clock.

Ken therefore compares altering his soda to a quarterback “spiking” a football.

“This not rum punch” clarifies that although the drink has been altered, he isn’t talking about simply adding rum to make an alcoholic punch—the song’s other drug references suggest something different has been added to the soda.

Ken names two recognizable diamond cuts rather than simply saying his jewelry contains diamonds.

Baguette-cut diamonds are elongated rectangular stones, while an emerald cut is generally rectangular with cropped corners and step-cut facets. Despite the name, an “emerald-cut diamond” is still a diamond—the term describes its cut rather than the gemstone itself.

The specificity continues the track’s obsession with high-end fashion and jewelry: Ken isn’t merely flexing diamonds, but particular styles of stones.
